criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The source count reaches the HD line on paper — six full entries (Bertram 2010, Ko 2007, Pascarella 2018, Dourish & Bellotti 1992, Whitson 2018, Maddila 2023), all peer-reviewed, all on one theme — and the entries genuinely answer my pet peeve rather than restating titles: 'One participant said "often bugs that are that critical don't even get filed because by the time that you would go to file it, the bug is already resolved" (P05, p. 296), so the most urgent work leaves the least trace' is exactly the specificity I asked for, and 'At A1 I labelled this mechanism articulation failure; on Whitson's evidence it is narrower — opacity, plus blame that lands on the tool' shows a source actually changing the author's mind. Three things hold it out of HD. (1) The review cannot motivate a project the reader has not yet been told about: the Introduction ends 'The research question this gap motivates is set out in Scoping Evidence', so 1,130 words of review are read before anyone knows what is being built, for whom, or what the question is. HD says the review motivates the project; this one motivates a project held offstage. (2) The synthesis rests load-bearing weight on a source that is never reviewed — 'A third reading disconfirms both: Washburn et al.'s (2016) 22-category scheme, derived from 155 postmortems, contains no communication category' is the pivot of the whole argument and Washburn gets no entry, no description, no usefulness statement. (3) The synthesis closes on 'Separating those predictions is what this study is for' and never does what the template asks of it — name the gap in the author's own learning, or say why the problem is current and topical for the games industry. The currency argument is stranded up in the Introduction, so the argument graph breaks at its most important joint. Density compounds all three: the Maddila entry packs a gradient-boosting model, a 24-hour gate, a string-matching heuristic and a three-arm trial into consecutive clauses, and cites 'Table 1's features' — a table in someone else's paper that I cannot see. That paragraph gets read twice, and under my own instruction that weakens the criterion it sits in.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Give Washburn et al. (2016) a full ~150-word entry in place of the 'At the edges' sentence about Stray and Mahaney, and rewrite the closing synthesis so it ends on the gap in the author's own learning plus one sentence on why the problem is live for game studios right now — then the review is six reviewed sources whose synthesis motivates a project the reader already understands.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: The mechanics are the best part of this draft and they are D-grade or better. Four learning goals span understand to create, each carries a measure, and they read as capabilities not achievements — 'Each is a CV line, not a thing I made: judging what a team's artefacts can and cannot tell you, then saying so to people who never open the repository, is daily production work' is precisely the framing I asked for, with the career motive attached. The methodology is genuinely mixed (Wilcoxon-scored comprehension items at Endsley's three levels, plus coded think-aloud with a second coder on 25%), the Kickstarter tiering is there ('L1, committed… L2, stretch… L3, challenge'), out-of-scope is named, the hour table sums to exactly 65 with in-prac summing to 15, and the variance against A1 is explained. What keeps it off HD is that the feasibility argument fails on the two points a sceptical marker tests first. First, the corpus: 'No single public Unity repository satisfies both legs of the fusion… The asset layer is therefore studied on RE-SS3D/SS3D and the tracker layer on immersivecognition/unity-experiment-framework, a composed corpus at a stated cost to ecological validity.' The entire thesis is the fusion of tracker, repository and asset signals, and the proposal concedes it has no corpus where the fusion can be demonstrated — then moves on without saying what that costs the claim or how the evaluation survives it. Naming a cost is not paying it. Second, the participants: eight readers and six think-alouds are priced at 20 hours, but the proposal never says who a 'producer-proxy' is, where the eight come from, or how they are briefed into the role — and the whole project history says producers are the unreachable population. A scoping section whose job is to convince of feasibility leaves its hardest recruitment question unasked. Smaller cracks: Deliverable 1 prices four heuristic evaluations, ≥25 review codings, ≥10 job ads and 'continued interviews' at 16 hours, which is not a credible estimate (the template's own worked study is 32); the job-ad scan appears once in the Introduction, vanishes, and resurfaces only as a table cell; the 'three-hour reservoir' gating L3 appears in no row of the 65-hour table, so the tiers and the hours are two unreconciled plans; and the Create goal's measure, 'four of six think-aloud participants… (A1's three of four, rescaled to the larger sample)', is not a rescaling — 3/4 is 75%, 4/6 is 67% — so the one goal that fixes the project's success threshold quietly lowers it while claiming continuity.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Devote one paragraph in Scoping Evidence to the split-corpus objection — state what the composed corpus can and cannot demonstrate about fusion, and name the participants and their recruitment route in the same breath — so the feasibility argument answers its own two weakest points instead of conceding them.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Structure, register and referencing are good: the template's sections are followed exactly, APA is consistent across nineteen entries, the body sits around 2,435 words inside the 2,499 ceiling, five figures plus a mechanism table are planned, and there are effectively no spelling or grammatical errors. But D requires the report to be 'very easy to read' and this one is not easy to read at all — it repeats the exact defect the A1 marker named ('So much information in each slide… You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context'). There is no plain overview anywhere: the document never states in one repeatable sentence what is being built and for whom, and the nearest thing to it is buried 1,400 words in ('A developer runs the tool; the producer reads the page and never opens Unity'). Sentences that must be read twice are systemic, not local: 'Nudge predicts a pull request's completion time by gradient boosting over Table 1's features, then applies an activity-detection gate — a fixed 24-hour recency test over state changes, comments and pushed commits — that suppresses the alert while work is still moving; state changes are themselves inferred by matching the word "voted" in comment text' is fifty-five words and four unfamiliar objects; 'Whether producer job advertisements reward this synthesis skill, the planned job-ad scan will test' is inverted for no gain; 'GitHub's squash-merge default appends the pull-request number to commit subjects, so a raw #N count returns 112, 81 and 40 for open-brush, VRTK and jynew against zero genuine issue references' arrives with no signpost for why it matters. Terms are used before definition throughout — 'every violation' in the Understand goal precedes any mention of heuristic evaluation; SQ1/SQ2, L1/L2/L3, 'team-week', 'producer-proxy' and 'activity-matched windows' are never expanded. Twelve parenthetical section references into other authors' papers (§3.1, §6.3, §4.1–4.3, Table 1) add apparatus a reader without those PDFs cannot use. Four cross-references to A1 ('as at A1', 'Against A1's table', 'A1's three of four') assume a document not in front of the marker. Telegraphic openers ('Two limits attach.' 'Three boundaries remain.') make the prose read as compressed notes. On referencing, Nielsen (1994) is listed but cited nowhere in the body. Torn between CR and D, I report CR, because the readability failure is the same one that cost twenty-seven marks on A1 and it is present in every section.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Open the Introduction with three plain sentences — what a producer is, what the tool does, what the research question is — and then split the four worst paragraphs (Maddila entry, Corpus, Ko's seven-category list, the L1/L2/L3 block) into shorter sentences with every term defined on first use, spending the ~60 words of word-count headroom on clarity rather than more evidence.

marker_malcolm.notes:
Weighted arithmetic: 0.45x78 + 0.40x76 + 0.15x68 = 35.1 + 30.4 + 10.2 = 75.7, reported as 76.

What the draft objectively earns, quoted: (a) six full source entries against the HD count, each closing on a usefulness sentence as the template demands — "It sets this proposal's premise: the record is incomplete before any tool reads it"; "give the think-aloud arm its coding frame"; "It bounds my novelty claim and defines what is left to contribute"; (b) an entry that shows a source changing the author's mind rather than confirming him — "At A1 I labelled this mechanism articulation failure; on Whitson's evidence it is narrower — opacity, plus blame that lands on the tool"; (c) learning goals that are capabilities not achievements, with the career line attached — "Each is a CV line, not a thing I made"; (d) the Kickstarter tiering I asked for, verbatim in shape — "L1, committed… L2, stretch… L3, challenge: absence detection, with a three-hour reservoir which an L1 over-run consumes first"; (e) an hour table that sums to exactly 65 with in-prac summing to exactly 15; (f) a genuinely mixed methodology with a named overtrust control — "One item is unanswerable from that condition's report, with a 'the report doesn't tell me' option as an overtrust detector"; (g) named rejected alternatives in three places, including "A multi-cutoff backtest was considered and rejected: a weekly report makes no forecast"; (h) an unusually strong Statement on Generative AI use that declares three AI-introduced errors caught by verification, which is evidence of process rather than an admission.

Calibration reasoning made explicit, per instruction. Two criteria were genuinely borderline and both were reported at the lower band. Literature Review sits at the HD source count but was marked D because the review motivates a project the reader has not been told about and rests on an unreviewed source at its pivot. Communication was the hardest call: structure, register and referencing are D-or-better, but the rubric's readability ladder is the axis this marker demonstrably weights, and the A1 result (Presentation 55 against an AI prediction of 82, with density and a missing overview as the entire written comment) shows the penalty is severe and this draft reproduces the defect in every section. CR 68 rather than D is the deliberate consequence of that calibration; if the Introduction gains a plain overview and the four densest paragraphs are broken up, Communication moves to 78-80 on its own and the task mark moves to roughly 80-82 once items 1, 3 and 5 are done.

Scope note: [FIGURE ...] placeholders were marked as figures that will exist, per instruction. That treatment materially rescues Scoping Evidence — without Figures 1 and 2 the section would fall to CR or below, since the draft's own fallback route is explicitly not a technical prototype on the intended tools with supporting images. The FALLBACK block was ignored as instructed but its existence is a live delivery risk on the criterion worth 40%.

Mechanical traps outside the assessed text, flagged because the Communication band grades "other submission requirements": Student ID unfilled, project title not chosen among three candidates, Topic Category unconfirmed against the real cover field, template instruction text and the Draft notes section still present, and the TOC field state unknown because the text extraction cannot see field codes.

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The source base itself is at HD level and I want to say so: six distinct, peer-reviewed, non-overlapping sources (Bertram CSCW 2010, Ko ICSE 2007, Pascarella MSR 2018, Dourish & Bellotti CSCW 1992, Whitson New Media & Society 2018, Maddila TOSEM 2023) on one theme, so the HD clause 'including academic research articles' is satisfied outright, and the specificity is exactly what I ask for — 'The causal need "what code caused this program state?" was the most frequently unsatisfied, failing in 61% of cases with searches of up to 21 minutes (§6.3), and its sources were the debugger and logs rather than colleagues, so that bottleneck is tool inadequacy' is a real potted summary, not a title restated. Rejected paths are used properly too: 'That remedy makes reporting easier; I do not take it, because it still asks the under-reporting party to report.' What stops it being HD is that 'expertly summarised' has to mean a marker reads it once. Several entries do not survive one pass — 'Nudge predicts a pull request's completion time by gradient boosting over Table 1's features, then applies an activity-detection gate — a fixed 24-hour recency test over state changes, comments and pushed commits — that suppresses the alert while work is still moving; state changes are themselves inferred by matching the word "voted" in comment text.' The section also opens cold on 'Bertram et al. (2010) studied issue tracking in four small, collocated software teams' with no sentence telling me what body of work I am about to read or how the six are organised, which is the same context failure that cost the A1 presentation its Content mark. And the synthesis leans a disconfirming argument on a seventh source that was never reviewed or evaluated: 'A third reading disconfirms both: Washburn et al.'s (2016) 22-category scheme, derived from 155 postmortems, contains no communication category.' Three defects of that weight put it in the lower half of D, not at HD.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Open the Literature Review with a 60–80 word orienting paragraph that names the one question the six sources are being asked (why does the shared production artefact under-report state?) and the three mechanism camps the reader is about to meet, then break the four longest sentences in the Ko, Dourish & Bellotti and Maddila entries into two each — so every entry reads correctly on the first pass and the synthesis lands as a conclusion the reader was prepared for rather than a compression.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: Three of the four sub-clauses are strong. The research question — 'Which of a producer's information needs can be answered automatically from the artefacts a team already produces — and which can't?' — is clear and genuinely insightful, and SQ1 is honestly framed as 'the insurance against a null result'. The methodology is properly mixed, not mixed in name: a within-subjects counterbalanced quantitative arm with an overtrust item and 'Per-item confidence (0–100) is never pooled with accuracy', against a think-aloud arm coded deductively with a second coder on 25%, and it declares its own limit — 'at n = 8 only large effects are detectable, a stated limitation'. The deliverables table gives all seven items a success measure, sums to exactly 65 with 15 in-prac, and the L1/L2/L3 tiering with a three-hour reservoir is the stretch-goal structure I want. What blocks HD is 'achievable' and 'strongly convincing argument for the feasibility', and the hole is in the study, not the software. The proposal never says who the eight participants are, where they come from, how they are recruited, or how long a session runs — 'Within-subjects, counterbalanced, n = 8' arrives with no sampling frame at all, and 'a producer-proxy's comprehension' is the closest thing to a participant definition anywhere in the document. Second, instrument design is neither budgeted nor ordered: every worked example in the template prices protocol and instrument design as its own line (3–7 h) before collection, whereas here Deliverable 3 is 'The evaluation, run' and the instruments appear only inside Deliverable 4, 'Evaluation report, instruments, de-identified data', at 7 h alongside the write-up — you cannot score six ground-truth items at three Endsley levels that have not been written and piloted. Third, the fidelity check that 'gates' both arms has no slot in the Week 11/12/13 schedule and no separate hours, despite the draft itself conceding 'the corpus's commit messages read "Fixed bugs", so a week's events must be read out of the diffs rather than off the log'. Fourth, Deliverable 1 prices four heuristic evaluations, 25+ reviews, 10+ job ads, continued interviews and a full need classification at 16 hours, which is the least credible number in the table and it is the line carrying the mandated UX-research direction. Four feasibility gaps in the evaluation is a pattern, not a slip, so this sits at the low end of D.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Add a 60–80 word Participants and instruments paragraph to Scoping Evidence naming the pool (e.g. COMP3151 student producers and teammates briefed into the producer role), the recruitment route, the per-session length and the pilot, and re-cut the hour table so protocol/instrument design and the two-week fidelity check are their own priced rows completed before Week 12 — feasibility then rests on a schedule rather than on an assertion.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Structure and compliance are the strong half: the document follows the template headings exactly, the body is ~2,419 words against the 2,499 ceiling excluding references, the APA list is consistent with DOIs throughout, and the sub-arms are properly signposted ('Quantitative arm.' / 'Qualitative arm.' / 'Corpus.' / 'Prototype.'). But D requires 'very easy to read' and this is not. The Introduction's fourth sentence runs 78 words across four semicolon-joined product clauses — 'No commercially available or open-source tool performs the full fusion of tracker state, repository history and engine/asset signals into a state description for a non-technical producer: McShaffry (2013) taught manual Perforce log-mining for producers; ZeroStandup turns tracker and repository activity into manager language but stops at engineers; …' — and the sentence before it is a grammatical inversion I had to read twice: 'Whether producer job advertisements reward this synthesis skill, the planned job-ad scan will test.' Nowhere in 2,400 words is there a plain sentence saying what ChangeLens is and what it does for whom; the reader must reconstruct it from the prototype paragraph on the third page. That is the A1 comment — 'It was hard to know what the presentation was about' — reproduced in prose. On the mechanical side: the figure sequence is 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 with no Figure 3, and Figures A, 4 and 5 are never referred to anywhere in the body, so three of the six 'relevant supporting images' float unanchored; Nielsen (1994) is in the reference list but cited nowhere in-text. Those are more than 'a few minor' referencing slips once counted together, and only the genuinely clean structure keeps this out of P.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Insert a plain-language opening paragraph (≤60 words, no jargon, no citations) in the Introduction stating what the tool is, who reads its output and what the project will test, then split the two Introduction sentences named above and add an in-text reference for every figure while renumbering the set 1–6 with no gap.

Weighted arithmetic: 0.45 × 78 + 0.40 × 75 + 0.15 × 70 = 35.1 + 30.0 + 10.5 = 75.6, reported as 76.

Scope assessed: the body between the markers (Introduction through Deliverables), the References list and the Statement on Generative AI use. All [NOTE, [DRAFT NOTE, [FALLBACK and [RB-CONFIRM lines and the Draft notes section were excluded, and [FIGURE …] placeholders were treated as figures that will exist.

Word count verified independently: body ≈2,419 words excluding headings, figure placeholders, bracketed notes and the table separator row — inside the 2,499 ceiling excluding references, with ~80 words of headroom. Introduction 195 (target ~200 ✓), Literature Review ~1,118 (cap 1,350, 232 words of unused allowance), Project Proposal ~1,116 (guide ~900). Per-section counts are a breakdown, not limits, so the over-run in Project Proposal is not itself penalisable — and the 232 unused Literature Review words are where the orienting paragraph in priority 1 and the Washburn credential in priority 5 should be spent.

Deliverables arithmetic checks out: hours sum to exactly 65, in-prac column sums to exactly 15. Every one of the seven deliverables carries a success measure, which is a genuine compliance win — the weakest are #5 ('3–4 minutes; my contribution named in the first minute', a length plus a mention rather than a quality goal) and #7 ('All four goals addressed with evidence'), but both clear the rubric's 'measurable' bar.

Source tally against the HD clause: six full entries (Bertram 2010, Ko 2007, Pascarella 2018, Dourish & Bellotti 1992, Whitson 2018, Maddila 2023), all peer-reviewed, all distinct authors and venues, one common theme. Stray 2016 and Mahaney & Lederer 2003 appear in a one-line edge paragraph and are correctly not claimed as full sources ('noted but not relied on'). Washburn 2016 is the anomaly — see priority 5. The HD requirement 'including academic research articles' is met outright; the source base is not what holds the Literature Review below HD.

Negative sources and rejected paths are present and used well — the Bertram entry declines the simplified-filing remedy, 'A multi-cutoff backtest was considered and rejected: a weekly report makes no forecast', the Nudge entry bounds the novelty claim rather than inflating it, and the L1/L2/L3 tiering with a three-hour reservoir is the stretch-goal structure the unit asks for. These are the strongest evaluative moves in the document and should survive any trimming.

Calibration note. The gap between this prediction and what a real marker returns is most likely to open at Communication and at the Introduction, not at the Literature Review — the A1 marker's entire written comment was about density and missing context, and that defect is reproduced here in prose: no plain overview, a 78-word product sentence in the first 200 words, an inverted sentence that must be read twice, and a document that never states in one sentence what the tool is. Priorities 1 and 4 address that directly and are worth more than their arithmetic suggests. Where I was torn I reported lower: Literature Review was arguable at 82 and is reported at 78 on readability; Project Proposal was arguable at 78 and is reported at 75 on four separate evaluation-feasibility gaps; Communication was arguable at 74 and is reported at the CR anchor of 70 because three unreferenced figures, a figure-numbering gap and an uncited reference-list entry together exceed 'a few minor errors'.

Unassessed risks flagged for the orchestrator rather than marked: the cover page still carries '[RAPHAEL TO FILL]' for Student ID and three unchosen title candidates; the prototype (ChangeLens-lite) did not exist at draft time, so Figures 1 and 2 were assessed on the instruction to treat placeholders as figures that will exist — if the prototype is not built, the fallback paragraph substitutes measurement for software and, as the draft itself concedes, does not meet the stated 'hello world of that tool' scoping bar, which would cost a further band on Project Proposal. The Statement on Generative AI use is unusually strong and should not be softened — declaring three caught AI-introduced errors as evidence of independent verification is the right posture — but it still contains two [RB-CONFIRM] claims that must be made true before submission.

cold_reader.what_is_it: ChangeLens is an automated report generator that fuses issue-tracker data, git commit history, and Unity asset signals into a single producer-readable summary, solving the core problem that commit volume and file counts bear almost no relationship to actual game development progress when most files are art, audio, or design rather than code.
cold_reader.who_is_it_for: Non-technical game producers and technical leads who need to assess project state and progress without reading the codebase themselves.
cold_reader.what_will_be_built: A Unity Editor package (ChangeLens-lite) that reads git history and categorizes file changes by type, a one-page report template tested in two conditions (tracker+repo only versus tracker+repo+asset signals), supported by a portfolio video, development diary, and evaluation report documenting the study findings.
cold_reader.what_will_be_measured: Whether non-technical producers can accurately answer comprehension questions about project state (what changed, what it means, what happens next) from the report alone; whether including asset-layer signals improves accuracy compared to tracker+repo only; and which categories of producer information needs can be answered automatically from existing artifacts versus requiring human judgment.

cold_reader.plain_opening: ChangeLens is a tool that automatically generates a weekly report for non-technical game producers, summarizing what their development team actually accomplished by reading the issue tracker, git commits, and game-engine asset files—since commit volume alone tells almost no truth about progress. Today this translation from code to producer language happens manually and inconsistently, done by a technical lead on demand at a high cost; the tool automates it by detecting what changed in code, art, design, and sound files simultaneously. The creator will test whether producers can actually use such a report to answer real questions about project state (what changed, what it means, what consequences follow) without ever opening the codebase, comparing a version that includes asset data against one without it. Success means the asset-layer signals improve producer understanding enough to be worth building into a production workflow, and that every claim the report makes holds up against the team's actual records.

questions.question: You differentiate ZeroStandup and P4 MCP purely by audience — "stops at engineers", "for developers rather than producers". Name the computation your tool performs that theirs does not, without referring to who reads the output.
questions.where_or_gap: The Nudge entry does give a mechanism boundary ("never composed across items"), but the Introduction's two live commercial rivals are separated only by audience label. Nothing in the body states a computation ZeroStandup or P4 MCP cannot perform, so the novelty claim collapses into a UI-for-producers claim — exactly the failure the dossier's Nudge position warns against.
questions.closing_sentence: Neither ZeroStandup nor P4 MCP reaches the Unity asset layer: mine names changed prefabs and scenes as objects from YAML `m_Name` and component GUIDs.

questions.question: A developer has to open your Editor window every week to produce a page only the producer reads. Dourish and Bellotti — your own source — say that exact arrangement is what fails. Why is yours exempt?
questions.where_or_gap: The role split is stated verbatim ("A developer runs the tool; the producer reads the page and never opens Unity"), but the draft never reconciles that manual invocation with the structural mechanism it builds the aggregation layer on — the reporter bearing a cost repaid to the group. The passive-by-product claim is asserted for the artefacts, never for the act of running the tool.
questions.closing_sentence: The developer runs one Editor command over a git log export; nothing is authored or judged by them, so Dourish and Bellotti's reporter cost does not arise.

questions.question: You claim object-level naming from prefab YAML is what makes the tool need Unity rather than a Python script — yet Figure 4 exists precisely to show those names sit in text Unity already versions. Why Unity?
questions.where_or_gap: The L1 sentence asserts the Unity dependency, and Figure 4's own caption undercuts it by proving the names are recoverable from versioned text. The only genuinely in-engine signal named anywhere is `BuildReport`, and that sits at L2 as a stretch goal, so the committed scope has no stated engine dependency.
questions.closing_sentence: YAML parsing needs no engine — Unity earns its place at L2, where `BuildReport` gives in-engine signal depth no external script can read.

questions.question: With eight readers, a six-item instrument and one deliberately unanswerable item, what difference could you actually detect — and what does a non-significant Wilcoxon licence you to say?
questions.where_or_gap: Analysis: Wilcoxon signed-rank with rank-biserial effect size, smallest

questions.question: Where do eight producer-proxies come from in Weeks 9 to 13, who recruits them and when, and what is the plan if five turn up?
questions.where_or_gap: No recruitment source, timeline or contingency appears anywhere in the body. The quantitative arm asserts n = 8, the qualitative arm "six of the same participants", and Deliverable 3 prices sixteen scored readings — but the only participant pool hinted at is the COMP3151 producer role mentioned in Learning Goals, and no fallback is stated if the number is not met.
questions.closing_sentence: The eight come from my COMP3151 cohort, briefed into the producer role; if fewer arrive I run the six think-alouds first, since SQ1 insures against a null result.

questions.question: Ethics gets one clause. Under what approval do you record eight participants thinking aloud on a set task, and what happens to the data of someone who withdraws halfway through a session?
questions.where_or_gap: The ethics line names five practices (public corpus, verbal consent, coded participants, no activity monitoring, no raw audio published) but no approval pathway, no withdrawal procedure and no retention or destruction rule. For a study whose entire qualitative arm is recorded human speech, that is a single clause carrying a whole governance question.
questions.closing_sentence: Participation is voluntary and consent verbal, so anyone may stop mid-session; their coded record is destroyed and only de-identified data reaches Deliverable 4.

questions.question: Your prototype classifies paths by extension and sibling `.meta`. It never opens a prefab. What exactly has it demonstrated about the object-level naming L1 commits to at sixty percent?
questions.where_or_gap: The Prototype paragraph describes a window that reads a `git log --name-status` export and buckets paths — file-level work. The committed L1 capability is YAML `m_Name` and GUID parsing, and no stated scoping evidence touches it. Figures 1 and 2 show the extension classifier; Figure 4 shows the YAML, but as a hand-annotation rather than as anything the tool has executed.
questions.closing_sentence: Figure 4 is that evidence: an annotated prefab hunk from the corpus showing `m_Name` and component GUIDs sit in text, so the parser has a known target.

questions.question: Deliverable 1 buys four heuristic evaluations, twenty-five reviews, ten job ads, continued interviews and a classification of every surfaced need — in sixteen hours. Show me the arithmetic.
questions.where_or_gap: The hour table is justified only by its delta from A1 ("the study falls to 16 because the tool sample is fixed at four and review mining is time-boxed"), never by a unit rate. No per-tool, per-review or per-interview cost is stated anywhere, so the totals are unauditable — and Deliverable 3's twenty hours must absorb six think-alouds, sixteen scored readings and a two-week hand-authored fidelity check that the text itself calls the largest estimation risk.
questions.closing_sentence: Deliverable 1 is time-boxed, not open-ended: four tools at the pilot pass's measured rate, with review and job-ad mining capped at the stated minimums.

questions.question: Your research question is about fusion, yet the asset layer and the tracker layer are measured on different repositories. Which repository generates the two reading conditions, and what does the other one actually contribute to the study?

confirmed_ok: Bertram et al. (2010) studied issue tracking in four small, collocated software teams (fifteen participants, interviews and questionnaires).
Their central finding is that the tracker is a hub for communication and coordination rather than a bug database.

One participant said "often bugs that are that critical don't even get filed because by the time that you would go to file it, the bug is already resolved" (P05, p. 296), so the most urgent work leaves the least trace.
Bertram et al. show the tracker under-recording at entry: filing is slower than fixing, and field-heavy forms deter non-technical filers.

readability.overview_first_opening: ChangeLens turns a Unity game project's history into a plain-language change report for producers. It is for non-technical producers, who now rely on a tech lead to translate commit history, expensively and inconsistently. It matters to game studios because most of what changes in a game project is not code, so tracking commits alone misses most of the real work. The project builds a small Unity editor tool that generates these reports, then tests whether producers understand a project better when the report includes changed assets, not just code.

products.name: ZeroStandup
products.what_it_says_now: Homepage markets itself as "The Standup meeting that writes itself": it "automatically fetches activity from version control systems, and project management tools to generate smart AI summaries. Zero manual input. Zero friction." Confirmed data sources: GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/Azure DevOps (repo) + Jira/Trello/Asana/ClickUp (tracker), plus Slack/Discord/Teams/calendars/Figma. Output is auto-posted standup-style summaries pitched at managers/team leads/engineers ("concise, high-level bullets that managers and stakeholders actually understand"). No mention anywhere of Unity, any game engine, or binary/asset data.
products.evidence: Fetched https://zerostandup.com/ on 17 Sep 2026. Verbatim: "automatically fetches activity from version control systems, and project management tools to generate smart AI summaries"; audience framed as managers/team leads/engineers. products.name: HacknPlan
products.what_it_says_now: Positions itself explicitly as a game-team PM tool: "Plan smarter, align every discipline, and ship great games faster"; "Run dedicated kanban boards for programming, art, design, audio, and production." State is driven by manual kanban/task entry across disciplines, not auto-derived from repo, build, or engine data. GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/Discord/Slack integrations exist but are described in terms of linking/notifications, not automated state extraction. No AI-generated narrative-report feature for producers is advertised on the page.
products.evidence: Fetched https://hacknplan.com/ on 17 Sep 2026. Confirms the draft's claim that HacknPlan 'recognises non-code disciplines but resolves them through manual entry.'

products.name: Perforce P4 MCP
products.what_it_says_now: Markets natural-language querying over Helix Core: "Your Source of Truth. Now Accessible Through Natural Language." Explicitly reads "complete version history for code and binary assets, with author and timestamp details" and project/file-level activity, plus P4 Code Review data (reviews, votes, workflows, comments). Framing is developer/technical-team facing ("Give your teams instant clarity into what's happening across projects", code review, merge-conflict resolution, reviewer recommendation). No mention of issue-tracker integration, producers, or non-technical-user capabilities anywhere on the page.
products.evidence: Fetched https://www.perforce.com/products/p4/p4-mcp on 17 Sep 2026. Confirms it narrates Helix Core history including binary assets for developers, not producers, and does not fuse in tracker/issue state — matching the draft's characterisation exactly.

new_threats.name: GitHub Copilot for Jira / Jira integration in the Copilot app
new_threats.what: GitHub Copilot's weekly release (published 10 Sep 2026) added a Jira integration to the Copilot app: "Bring Jira issues into a shared canvas, choose what moves forward, and let Copilot carry the context into investigation, implementation, and pull request preparation." This is a developer-workflow feature — Jira issues feed into Copilot's coding/implementation loop, not into a producer-facing status report.
new_threats.date: 10 Sep 2026 (within window; underlying 'GitHub Copilot for Jira' reached general availability 25 Jun 2026, outside window)
new_threats.fuses_tracker_repo_engine_for_producers: No — fuses Jira issue context into a developer's investigation/implementation/PR workflow inside Copilot. No narrative report is generated, no engine/asset-layer signal is read, and the flow terminates at the developer, not a non-technical producer. [uncertain: one auto-generated summary of this page described the audience as 'producers and managers', but that contradicts the page's own quoted text, which describes a developer-facing canvas feeding PR preparation — the developer-facing reading is treated as correct here.]
new_threats.impact: Does not undermine the draft's novelty claim. It extends the existing 'tracker+repo, engineer audience' category the draft already concedes to ZeroStandup; still no engine/asset fusion and still stops at engineers.

new_threats.name: Linear — "Draft Project Updates" (Linear Agent) and "Loops for Product Management"
new_threats.what: Linear shipped (3 Sep 2026) an agent feature that will "summarize progress, risks, blockers, and recent changes into an update your team can review and post," drawing on "your projects, issues, customer requests, docs, and code." A follow-on feature (14 Sep 2026), Loops, automates recurring workspace-triggered updates (e.g., when project dates shift) and can edit documents and post to Slack.
new_threats.date: 3 Sep 2026 (Draft Project Updates) and 14 Sep 2026 (Loops for Product Management)
new_threats.fuses_tracker_repo_engine_for_producers: Partial — fuses issue-tracker state with code/repo activity ("recent changes") into a narrative update; audience is the broader product team (engineers, EMs, PMs), not specifically framed as a non-technical producer. No mention of game engines, Unity, or binary/asset signals anywhere on the page.
new_threats.impact: Narrows the draft's tracker+repo→manager-language claim slightly further (a second vendor besides ZeroStandup now does this), but does not touch the engine/asset-layer gap the draft's novelty claim actually rests on. The Introduction's ZeroStandup sentence should be read as one instance of a now-two-vendor pattern rather than a singular exception; the underlying gap claim (no fusion of tracker + repo + engine/asset signals for a non-technical producer) is unaffected.

new_threats.name: Unity Production Pipeline (previewed at Unite Seoul, cloud production platform)
new_threats.what: Unity's cloud platform "connect[s] your whole production pipeline through a new API and a set of services, so each role can plug in their own tools," explicitly naming producers among the served roles: "Producers, artists, and QA review real game renders on the web or on device, not proxy screenshots." Supports GitHub and Unity Version Control integration (closed beta) and an "API and CLI built for agents to validate assets, fix issues, submit for review, and trigger builds." No description of fusing issue-tracker state with repo history into a narrative status report was found.
new_threats.date: Announced at Unite Seoul, 21 Jul 2026 (before the 1 Aug-17 Sep 2026 window); public availability targeted November 2026 (also outside the window); closed beta ongoing as of the fetch on 17 Sep 2026
new_threats.fuses_tracker_repo_engine_for_producers: No confirmed fusion — it is a review/asset-validation/build-trigger tool serving producers among other roles, not a tracker+repo+engine narrative-report generator. [uncertain: closed-beta feature set is not fully public; a fuller producer-reporting capability could exist behind the beta that the public page does not describe.]
new_threats.impact: Outside the strict 1 Aug-17 Sep 2026 announcement window (announced 21 Jul 2026), so it does not itself need to be added as an in-window threat, but it is the single closest thing to a 'Unity itself builds this' risk found and is worth one flagged sentence in the Introduction or a footnote, since it explicitly names producers as a served role for the first time among Unity's own tooling. As described today it does not perform the tracker+repo+engine fusion into a narrative report, so it does not defeat the novelty claim, but it should be watched: re-check at its November 2026 public release, which lands after A2 is due (20 Sep 2026) but before A3.
